title: The exposome in respiratory diseases: multiple preventable risk factors from early life to adulthood.
ehr_evidence: This journal club article reviews three recent publications investigating the effects of environmental exposures... using data from the INMA and RHINESSA cohorts... NutriNet-Santé cohort. The actual sources were prospective/retrospective cohort data, questionnaires, biospecimen assays (urine), and environmental monitoring/GIS, not EHR.
summary: Journal club commentary reviewing three cohort studies investigating the impact of environmental exposures (phthalates, air pollution, greenness, lifestyle factors) on respiratory health outcomes (lung function, asthma, rhinitis) from early life to adulthood.
key_findings: Gestational phthalate exposure associated with lower FVC and FEV1 in children, especially early childhood (e.g., FEV1 z-score coefficient at age 4: −0.024 for 10% increase in MiBP).
Air pollutants associated with increased risk of asthma attacks (adjusted OR 1.60–2.46), rhinitis, and impaired lung function.
Greenness not associated with asthma or rhinitis, but associated with impaired lung function (adjusted OR 1.68–1.53).
Three early-life and one lifestyle exposure profiles associated with increased risk of asthma symptoms (mean score ratio 1.11–1.96) and uncontrolled asthma (OR 1.45–2.88).
captured_features: air pollution levels (NO2, PM10, PM2.5, black carbon, O3)
study_design: journal club commentary reviewing cohort and cross-sectional studies
data_source_type: cohort study data, questionnaires, biospecimen assays, environmental monitoring, spirometry
population: mother-child pairs from Spain, adults from Norway and Sweden, and adults from France
exposure_domain: phthalates, air pollution, greenness, socioeconomic, early-life environment, lifestyle-anthropometric factors
limitations: small sample size and sociodemographic differences (INMA)
low response rate and selection bias (RHINESSA)
highly correlated exposures and lack of multi-pollutant models (RHINESSA)
health-conscious participant bias and lack of generalizability (NutriNet-Santé)
